opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so maybe I should start with what Timaeus is trying to do, since that frames everything else. We're a research organization, and our bet is that singular learning theory gives us the right mathematical foundation for understanding what's going on inside neural networks. Not just what they compute at the end of training, but how that structure forms along the way.

The basic observation behind SLT is that neural networks are singular models. The map from parameters to functions is highly degenerate: lots of different parameter settings implement the same function, and the geometry of the loss landscape near those solutions is very non-generic. Classical statistical learning theory mostly assumes this away. Sumio Watanabe's insight was that you can't assume it away, and that the degeneracy actually controls generalization and which solutions a learning process prefers. Quantities like the learning coefficient, or the real log canonical threshold, measure how degenerate a solution is, and in a precise sense they measure its effective complexity.

So I see our role as taking that body of theory, which was developed largely for Bayesian statistics and came from algebraic geometry, and making it actually usable for deep learning, and specifically for alignment. That breaks down into a few pieces.

First, there's the empirical and engineering work of turning theoretical quantities into things you can estimate on real models. A lot of our early effort went into the local learning coefficient: building estimators using SGLD-style sampling, checking that they behave the way theory predicts on toy models where we know the answer, and then scaling them up to transformers. If you can't measure it, the theory stays a nice story.

Second, there's what we call developmental interpretability. The idea is that if you watch training through the lens of SLT, you see that models don't learn smoothly. They go through something like phase transitions, distinct developmental stages where the geometry changes and new structure crystallizes. In small language models trained on in-context tasks, for example, you can detect these stage boundaries with the learning coefficient and related tools, and they line up with the model acquiring qualitatively new capabilities. That's exciting from an alignment perspective, because it suggests you could detect when something important is being learned, rather than only auditing the finished model.

Third, and this is where we've been increasingly focused, is connecting structure in the model back to structure in the data. If you want to align a model, ultimately you're shaping it through data and training. So the question is: which parts of the training data are responsible for which internal structures and behaviors? We've been developing SLT-inspired tools, things like susceptibilities and other ways of probing how the posterior responds to perturbations of the data distribution, that let you start to attribute internal structure to data. If that works, it starts to look less like interpretability as pure observation and more like a lever you can pull.

Zooming out, the reason I think this matters for alignment is that our current situation is that we train these systems and hope they generalize the way we want. We lack a science of how training data, architecture, and optimization together determine what a model internalizes. SLT is, as far as I can tell, the most promising candidate for the mathematical core of that science. Timaeus's job is to push it from a beautiful theory into a practical toolkit: validate it, scale it, and build the bridge to concrete alignment applications like detecting dangerous capabilities as they emerge, understanding generalization, and eventually steering it.

I should be honest that a lot of this is still early. There are real open questions about how well the theory transfers to the regime of very large models trained with SGD rather than Bayesian sampling, and about how reliable our estimators are at scale. But the results so far have been encouraging enough that I think it's one of the better bets in the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So Timaeus, which I think is what you're pointing at, was set up basically to take singular learning theory, which had mostly been a fairly niche corner of mathematical statistics thanks to Sumio Watanabe's work, and turn it into something you can actually run on real neural networks and connect to the alignment problem.

The way I'd put the role is in a few pieces. The first is just engineering: SLT gives you quantities like the local learning coefficient, which tells you about the effective dimensionality or degeneracy of a model around a given solution, but on paper that's defined through integrals you can never compute. A lot of our early work was figuring out how to estimate it with SGLD-style sampling at the scale of transformers, and checking that the estimates behave sensibly, that they track the things the theory says they should. Without that, it's a nice theory with nothing to say about GPT-sized models.

The second piece is science. Once you have those estimators, you can watch training and ask: where are the phase transitions, when does the model's internal structure change discontinuously, and what's being learned at those moments? We've done this on toy models of superposition, on small language models learning in-context learning, and the picture that keeps showing up is that training looks much more like a sequence of discrete developmental stages than a smooth slide down a loss curve. That's interesting on its own, but it matters for alignment because the things we care about, like whether a model picks up a deceptive strategy or some generalization we didn't intend, are presumably structural changes of exactly this kind. If you can detect them, you have at least a shot at intervening before they're locked in.

The third piece is the longer-term bet, which is that interpretability needs a theory of what structure is and how it forms, not just tools for poking at a finished model. SLT is the best candidate we know of for that. The geometry of the loss landscape, the way singularities organize which solutions are reachable and preferred, gives you a principled handle on why a network ends up with the circuits it has. Timaeus's job, as I see it, is to be the group that stays committed to that program long enough to find out whether it pays off, and to make the results legible to the rest of the alignment community so people can build on them rather than having to reconstruct the math from scratch.

I should be honest that we're early. The empirical results so far are on small systems, and there's a real question about how much of this survives contact with frontier-scale models. But I think the theory is unusually well-positioned, because the quantities it cares about are intrinsic to the model and the data, not to some particular probing method we happened to invent, and that's the kind of thing you want if you're trying to make safety claims that hold up.

astra-6.text:
I see TUS’s role as helping close the gap between singular learning theory as a mathematical framework and something we can actually use to understand neural networks.

There are two parts to that. One is developing the theory: understanding which aspects of a model’s structure matter for learning and generalization. The other is empirical: figuring out whether we can measure those things in real models, and whether those measurements tell us something that existing tools miss.

For alignment, the hope is that this gives us a better handle on how internal structure develops during training. Can we identify meaningful changes in what a model has learned? Can we understand why particular solutions are favored? Those are potentially useful ingredients for alignment, but there’s a substantial gap between having an interesting measure of complexity and being able to diagnose whether a model is safe. I see the contribution as building that foundation and testing how far it takes us.

sol-6.1.text:
I see TUS’s role as helping close the gap between singular learning theory as a mathematical framework and something we can actually use to understand neural networks. There’s a lot of promise in the idea that the geometry of the loss landscape tells us something about which solutions learning will favor. But turning that into useful predictions about real models is a substantial research program.

For alignment, I’d want us to make those connections concrete. Can we detect meaningful changes in what a model has learned? Can we distinguish different kinds of generalization, even when the models look similar on the training data? And can we do that reliably enough to inform decisions about training or deployment?

I don’t think singular learning theory gives us an alignment solution by itself. The opportunity is to develop a better science of learning, with mathematical ideas and experiments constraining each other, and then establish which parts of that science actually help with alignment.
